utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the Registrar call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Case number IT-00-39-PT, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'll hear the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Brenda Hollis and Nicola Piacente appear for the Prosecution, assisted by Carmela Annink-Javier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NESKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, but first and foremost, I can't find the right channel. I can't hear the interpretation. Good morning. I'm Goran Neskovic, and I'm Defence counsel for Mr. Krajisnik. Could you please help me, because there seems to be something wrong with the channel. Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is the postponed Status Conference in this case. The various matters which I have in mind to discuss are these: First of all, dealing with the application for joinder of this case with the case of Biljana Plavsic, a timetable for that; to discuss then pre-trial preparations; the status and condition of the accused; and any other matters which may arise, including fixing a date for the next Status Conference. The Trial Chamber has received the Prosecution application dated the 23rd of January. Mr. Neskovic, you will have 14 days to respond, of course, to that motion, unless you want to give a response immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. NESKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I haven't received any papers concerning the application for joinder, and I do realise that the deadline is 14 days for giving a response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, no doubt a copy can be handed to counsel today. Have the Prosecution got a copy? The Court's got a copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Plus, Your Honour, it's our understanding that there may be a copy of it already in Mr. Neskovic's locker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Well, Mr. Neskovic, no need to react to that for the moment. There is the application, and you've got 14 days to respond to it. This application having been made, the target date which I mentioned at the last hearing cannot be met and must be vacated, at least for the moment. The Trial Chamber will, of course, have to determine the motion and determine whether these cases should be joined or not, but pending that ruling, there can be no date fixed for any trial. I also have in mind that there is one appeal outstanding in relation to jurisdiction and that has yet to be resolved. When those matters are resolved, then a further timetable could be set, but the target date will have to be vacated, as I say. One matter I note from the Notice of Motion and that is that an estimate appears for the Prosecution case of a joint trial, stating that the complex cases, as indeed they would be, will require a lengthy trial, very possibly two or more years for the entire trial. That, of course, I understand, is an estimate and no more than a reference to a possibility, but the length of trial of two years is unacceptable, and the Prosecution must, of course, have that in mind when preparing for the trial. Ms. Hollis, can you assist with the preparations as far as this trial is concerned? On the last occasion when the case was before the Court, there was talk of 78 witnesses having been identified. As far as the witnesses are concerned, is this matter now in hand?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have since that time contacted all of the confirmation witnesses to determine their availability. Most of those witnesses have indicated that they will be available to testify. Also, since that time, we have disclosed witness statements and documentary evidence in relation to 29 of the 41 municipalities that are at issue. Since the last Status Conference, we have disclosed to the Defence approximately 14.000 pages of documents pertaining to both witness information and hard copies of documentary evidence. In addition to that, we have provided to the Defence approximately 25 CD-ROMs that would contain about 85.000 pages of documentary evidence. We have also, since that time, been progressing in the overall searches that we told the Court about. It is estimated that by the end of June, we will have completed 80 to 82 per cent of the searches of the total of 2.7 million pages. The remaining 18 to 20 per cent are not searchable because of problems with the quality of the documents and also problems we have because of the B/C/S and Cyrillic. We're hoping to overcome those problems so that eventually we'll be able to provide the results of a 100 per cent search, but at this time, it appears by the end of June we will have gone through 80 to 82 per cent of that 2.7 million. And as I explained earlier, as the initial search is done and documents are identified as potentially relevant given the broad search criteria we provide, then a listing of those documents are submitted to the trial team. The trial then goes through and makes selections based on their potential use at trial as well as our obligations under Rule 68, and then as we determine either we may use them or we believe they may fall under Rule 68, those documents are then provided to the Defence. So when I speak to you of the CD-ROMs, very often we're providing disclosure by CD-ROM if it's a large document collection, hard copy if it is a smaller collection and we have determined that it is relevant. We understand that the disclosure to the Defence will be much broader than what we use at trial. We certainly took heed to Your Honours' words that we should use only the most relevant documents, but, of course, in order to determine that, we have to review the documents that are potentially relevant. So we are progressing on those fronts. In regard to the international witnesses that I spoke to you about the last time, to date we will have completed our interviews with 11 of 17 internationals who have been identified as potential witnesses. We have submitted a request for interview with the remaining six. However, we have not yet received approval from the relevant authorities for those interviews. So we continue to attempt to set up those six interviews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The 2.7 million documents are those which are potentially relevant; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: That's our total collection. Among those are duplicates. Those are weeded out at the early stages. There is an estimate that in our main database there's probably 1.7 million pages that are potentially relevant, and in our database that has to do with seized collections there's probably another 750.000 pages. So as we go through the searches, the duplications are weeded out. Those documents that clearly would have no relevance, for example, if we're looking for Ministry of Defence and the document is identified by Ministry of Defence and it turns out it's the Ministry of Defence for Great Britain, then that is excluded at that time. So we're narrowing as we go through our searches to get down to the pool that are potentially relevant, and then those are broken out according to further categories we have given the people. They come down to the team and we weed them out. So at this point in time in this case, of those ones that are potentially relevant, there is a final review rate of acceptance of about 24 to 30 per cent, and it is that amount that are sent down to the second echelon of reviewers who look at those in the context of our case to determine one, do they need to be disclosed under Rule 68; number two, are they potentially relevant for the case; and then based on those selections, the numbers are further reduced. So it's a funnel-type Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 approach to the issue, getting smaller as we work through the levels of review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What would the effect of a joinder be on this process?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We have had in mind the possibility of the accused Plavsic being here, as well as the fact that anything relevant to her activities is probably relevant to Mr. Krajisnik. So the search has encompassed both all along. So that would not prolong the search.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As far as witnesses are concerned, are there many in common?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Most of them will be in common, even at the international level. With the international witnesses, what we call, in general, the linkage witnesses, there may be some differences there because it could be that some people have had contact with only one of the two accused, but the great bulk of the witnesses in this case will be the crime-base witnesses and those would all be the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You must remind me what you mean by "linkage." Linkage with what?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: The witnesses who would establish why these particular accused should be held guilty for the crimes that occurred in Bosnia. So those could include the internationals that we're talking about, policy witnesses, also witnesses who will explain the responsibility and authority of the various organisations to which these accused belonged and in which they participated, experts to explain some of the issues, those types of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. On the last occasion there was talk of some meetings, and I gather there was some cooperation between the parties on presenting this case. Is there any further news on that?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We did not have meetings prior to this Status Conference, but we did have meetings prior to the other Status Conferences. We have been able to cooperate in setting up, if you will, a framework for cooperation. Since the last Status Conference, we have submitted an additional 34 adjudicated facts to the Defence for them to consider. To date, we have received no response from the Defence as to whether they would accept any of the adjudicated facts submitted, nor have we received a response as to which, if any, of the numbered parts of the indictment they might stipulate to or agree to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No doubt this matter can be taken further in terms of possible meetings. If not, it will have to be dealt with by the Trial Chamber formally.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm confident that we can -- we certainly can have additional meetings and discuss that. Perhaps the Defence is waiting for additional disclosure before they decide upon the adjudicated facts or the indictment, but we have worked well together, and I have every reason to believe we will continue to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any matters which the Prosecution want to raise?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, you've heard what's been said. Obviously, in due course, you should respond to the invitation to admit some adjudicated facts, and you should continue to meet with the Prosecution in order to present, if possible, an agreed framework for the trial. You've heard what's been said about disclosure. Obviously there's a large amount of material which is coming to you. As I said, the trial cannot now take place in May, but it must take place as soon as possible thereafter. Is there anything you want to say about cooperation with the Prosecution or indeed any other matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. NESKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as for admitting some adjudicated facts and as for the indictment itself, the Defence is working on this. Of course, there are quite a few problems involved because there are a lot of documents and this is quite a burden for the Defence. You heard that this is 2.7 million documents, as the Prosecutor said. If we look at all these documents that are being served upon the Defence, these are not only documents from the state government, from regional governments, town authorities, et cetera, but it goes all the way down to village guards. So in order to read all of this, at least, not to mention analyse it all substantively, the Defence would need five to ten attorneys. In this way, the Prosecutor has actually provided everything that exists in terms of documents from 41 towns in Republika Srpska. So these are -- so these are all the documents related to Republika Srpska. However, if the Defence were to deal with all the documents of this nature that were from the Muslim/Croat Federation, then that would be even more documents. You know that additional hours have been granted for the Defence and for its investigators in order to prepare properly. However, still we have problems related to documentation and studying it, and of course we have the constant problem of witnesses. As for the application for a joinder, I'm not going to say anything right now, but I think that Mr. Krajisnik and Ms. Biljana Plavsic, even according to the indictment, had different positions after all, because first the position of Ms. Biljana Plavsic will have to be determined, and after that the position of Mr. Krajisnik, both causes -- consequences in relation to both, and then the Defence will work in accordance with that. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As far as your resources are concerned dealing with these documents, you can make an application for a co-counsel, and obviously you should consider that. You may have done. You may have made the application. But clearly, more resources are going to be needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NESKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, we have submitted such a request and I expect that our team will finally have been established by mid-February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If at any stage you find difficulty about coping with the amount of work, then it's a matter you can raise with the Trial Chamber. We don't want to be in the position either of the Defence not being properly prepared - you must have the opportunity for that - but at the same time, we don't want to be holding the trial up because of lack of preparation. So keep, if you would, both those matters in mind in the coming preparation period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NESKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are there any other matters which you want to raise, Mr. Neskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NESKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. It remains to deal with the status and condition of the accused. Before I do that, the next Status Conference in this case must take place on or about the 25th of May. Now, it may be that before then there will be other considerations which will mean that an additional hearing will be necessary, but the 25th of May is the last possible date for the next Status Conference. Mr. Neskovic, is there anything that you want to raise or the accused wants to raise in connection with the conditions of detention? If there are, we'll go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NESKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing, Your Honour. Maybe perhaps Mr. Krajisnik, the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have something to say if I'm permitted to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into closed session.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
